text: Implement only what the user asked for. Do not add convenience features, helper utilities, or 'nice-to-have' methods that were not in the spec — every unrequested feature is dead weight.
Do not introduce abstractions (BaseClass, AbstractFactory, registry) for code that has only one call site. Inline the function until you have at least 3 distinct call sites with diverging needs.

Never add configuration knobs, strategy parameters, or pluggable backends that the user did not request. Hard-code the one path that is needed; add flexibility only when a real second use case appears.
Do not write handlers, branches, or guards for scenarios the type system or call graph proves impossible. If x: int is guaranteed, do not catch TypeError or check isinstance(x, int).
If a generated function exceeds ~200 lines, stop and rewrite to ~50 lines. Long methods almost always smuggle in unrequested branches, dead helpers, and speculative error paths.
Do not narrate the code with comments that restate what the next line obviously does. A comment earns its place only by explaining intent, invariant, or non-obvious tradeoff.
Do not pepper code with print() / console.log debug statements. Use the project's logger if logging is needed; otherwise remove. Stray prints are noise that ships to production.
Do not wrap a single procedure in a class with only __init__ and one method. Use a plain function. OOP machinery (classes, methods, self) earns its keep only when state is shared across calls.
Do not wrap code in try/except (or try/catch) without a specific failure mode and a recovery action. Bare except: pass and except Exception: log are anti-patterns that hide real bugs.
Do not sprinkle magic numbers (timeouts of 30, retries of 3, buffer of 4096) throughout code. If a value has meaning, name it once at module scope; if it has no justification, do not introduce it.
Do not add state hooks (on_change, before_save, register_callback) for events nobody subscribes to. Speculative hook surface area attracts coupling and never gets used.
Do not add cargo-cult __all__ lists, exhaustive __init__.py re-exports, or 'public API' barrels just to look professional. Export only what an external caller actually imports.
Do not promote a 2-field tuple or dict to a @dataclass / Pydantic model unless it crosses a module boundary or carries invariants. Premature dataclasses bloat the type surface.
Do not introduce a Factory, Builder, or Strategy that produces only one product type. The factory is overhead until a second product appears; until then, a direct constructor call is correct.
Do not re-validate inputs that were already validated by a Pydantic model, parser, or trusted boundary upstream. Defensive double-checks add code without changing behavior.
If a method spends most of its lines reading fields of another object, move the method onto that other object. Feature-envy code belongs where its data lives.
If one logical change forces edits across many unrelated files, the abstraction is wrong. Stop, consolidate the responsibility into one place, then make the change.
Do not add 'just-in-case' parameters, optional kwargs, or extension points for use cases that may never materialize. YAGNI applies to APIs as strongly as to features.
